nodes.text: Certain visions are reported which seem to bring into this discussion a question not to be neglected. For it is said that some of the dead have appeared, either in dreams or in some other way, to living people who did not know where their bodies lay unburied, and, showing them the places, have urged that the burial they had lacked be provided for them. If we reply that these things are false, we shall seem to go shamelessly against the writings of certain of the faithful and against the perceptions of those who affirm that such things have happened to them. But the answer must be that we are not to think the dead are aware of these things just because they seem in dreams to say or indicate or ask for them. For the living, too, often appear to the living as they sleep, while they themselves do not know that they appear; and they hear from them what they dreamed, as they say that they saw them in their dreams doing or saying something. If, then, someone can see me in a dream showing him something that has happened, or even foretelling something that is to come, while I am wholly ignorant of it and care not at all, not only about what he dreams, but whether he is awake while I sleep, or asleep while I am awake, or whether at one and the same time we are both awake or both asleep, when he sees the dream in which he sees me: what wonder is it if the dead, without knowing or perceiving these things, are nevertheless seen by the living in dreams and say something which, on waking, they find to be true? I would believe, then, that it is by the workings of angels, whether permitted or commanded from above, that they seem in dreams to say something about the burial of their bodies, when those whose bodies they are know nothing of it at all. And this sometimes happens usefully, either for some sort of comfort to the living, to whom those dead belong whose images appear to the dreamers, or so that by these admonitions the humane duty of burial may be commended to the human race, a duty which, though it does not help the departed, is nonetheless neglected only through blameworthy irreligion. Sometimes, however, men are thrown into great errors by deceptive visions, men whom it is just should suffer such things. As, for instance, if someone were to see in a dream what Aeneas, by poetic falsehood, is said to have seen in the underworld, and the image of some unburied person were to appear to him and say such things as Palinurus is said to have said to Aeneas; and when he woke he were to find the body in the place where, in his dream, he heard that it lay unburied, having been warned and asked to bury it when found; and, because he found this to be true, he were to believe that the dead are buried so that their souls may pass to the places from which, as he dreamed, the souls of the unburied are barred by a law of the underworld: does he not, believing this, stray very far from the path of truth?
